title: Building Everyday Resilience
hook: Resilience isn't a personality you're born with — it's a set of habits and connections you can build, the way you build a muscle.
key_points: Resilience is the ability to adapt and recover from adversity — and it can be learned.
Strong relationships and asking for support are the biggest protective factors.
Looking after the basics — sleep, movement, routine — builds your baseline capacity to cope.
Reframing how you think about a setback shapes how well you weather it.
content_html: We tend to admire resilient people as if they were made differently. The American Psychological Association's research says otherwise: resilience is largely built, through ordinary habits and relationships, and that means it's available to everyone.
extra_html: The APA defines resilience as the process of adapting well in the face of adversity, stress, or hardship — and is emphatic that it isn't a trait some lucky people are simply born with. Its guidance centers on a few buildable pillars. The strongest is connection: nurturing supportive relationships and accepting help, which buffers stress better than going it alone. Caring for the body — sleep, movement, and steady routines — raises your baseline ability to cope. So does how you think: viewing setbacks as temporary and surmountable, keeping things in perspective, and taking small, decisive actions rather than freezing. The encouraging part is that none of this requires a personality transplant; it's practice, and it compounds.

related.title: What Stress Does to Your Body
related.hook: A jolt of stress is useful — it sharpens you for a real threat. The problem is when the alarm never switches off, and the body pays for staying on high alert.

related.title: What Mental Health Really Means
related.hook: Mental health isn't just the absence of illness — it's being able to cope with life's stresses, work, learn, and contribute. Everyone has it, and it can be cared for.

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

flashcards.prompt: According to the APA, resilience is best understood as:

choices.text: A skill set that can be learned and strengthened
A fixed trait you either have or don't

flashcards.explanation_html: The APA describes resilience as the process of adapting well to adversity — something built through behaviors, thoughts, and actions anyone can develop.

flashcards.prompt: What does the APA call the single biggest protective factor for resilience?
flashcards.back_html: Connection — strong, supportive relationships and being willing to lean on them. Social support is the most consistently protective factor.
